Reproducing Armstrong & Vlasov (2026) from dandiset 001341¶

Paper. Armstrong AG, Vlasov Y (2026). Neural correlates of perceptual decision-making in the primary somatosensory cortex. PNAS 123(18), e2514107123. doi:10.1073/pnas.2514107123. The claims file was written from the accepted author manuscript in PubMed Central (NIHMS2207436, PMC13142948) and its SI Appendix.

Dandiset. DANDI:001341, version 0.260414.1316. The paper cites this version (reference 63, "Version 0.260414.1316", DOI 10.48324/dandi.001341/0.260414.1316), and it is the only published version; the draft has the same two assets. The files are streamed; nothing is downloaded.

What the dandiset holds. Two NWB files, animals 489 and 503 of the 19 in Table S1, each with the units table, the trials table and the ball tracking at 500 Hz. It holds no wall positions, whisker tracking, touch times, gait or psychometric sessions, and no synchronisation signal between the spike times and the trial clock, although the SI says LabVIEW TTL signals were used to synchronise the recordings with the behaviour (SI, Electrophysiological recordings).

Claims. From claims/001341/10.1073-pnas.2514107123.yaml. Six are tested; the others are blocked.

import time
import warnings
from multiprocessing import Pool

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import h5py
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy import stats

import barrel_vr as bv

pd.set_option("display.width", 200)
pd.set_option("display.max_columns", 40)
pd.set_option("display.max_rows", 200)
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")

started = time.time()
urls = bv.asset_urls()
S = {}
for s, u in urls.items():
    f = bv.open_session(u)
    tr = bv.load_trials(f)
    beh = bv.load_behaviour(f)
    seg = bv.trial_segments(beh)
    S[s] = dict(file=f, trials=tr, beh=beh, seg=seg, units=bv.load_units(f), spikes=bv.all_spikes(f),
                samples=bv.trial_table_from_samples(beh, seg))
print(f"dandiset {bv.DANDISET_ID} version {bv.DANDISET_VERSION}: sessions {list(S)}, "
      f"loaded in {time.time() - started:.0f} s")

dandiset 001341 version 0.260414.1316: sessions ['489', '503'], loaded in 11 s

Data check¶

Each check of the metadata against the values is stated under its output. First the session metadata and the contents of each file.

The sessions are 489 (2022-07-08) and 503 (2022-09-02), as in Table S1. The file of 489 gives its age as P63D, but its date of birth and session date are 68 days apart, which is the P68 of Table S1. For 503 the file says P89D and Table S1 P89; the dates are 88 days apart. Both files give a weight of 0.02 kg. Every acquisition series has a unit; trial (unit "n") is the trial number of each sample and ts_local the time since that trial started.

Next, the trials table against the sample series.

for s, d in S.items():
    tr = d["trials"]
    print(f"session {s}: {len(tr)} rows in the trials table; by label:", tr.label.value_counts().to_dict())
    print(f"  intact rows (before the first repeated start time): {tr.intact.sum()};",
          "by label:", tr[tr.intact].label.value_counts().to_dict())
    print(f"  rows with stop before start: {tr.negative.sum()} (all OL: {tr[tr.negative].label.str.startswith('OL').all()}),"
          f" rows {tr.index[tr.negative].min()} to {tr.index[tr.negative].max()}")
    it = tr[tr.intact]
    gap = it.start_time.values[1:] - it.start_time.values[:-1]
    neg = np.flatnonzero(it.negative.values[:-1])
    print(f"  for those rows, next start minus start: {np.round(np.unique(np.round(gap[neg], 3)), 3)} s")

In both sessions, a run of OL rows (62 in 489, 63 in 503) has a stop time earlier than its start time. The samples of these rows carry timestamps that restart at the preceding straight row's start, while ts_local runs from 0 to 2.0 s and the next row starts 2.0 s after the row's start. The start times are therefore taken as right, the timestamps and stop times of those rows as wrong, and time within a trial is taken from ts_local. All other intact rows start at their first sample's timestamp.

In 489, the trials table from row 1000 on (611 rows) repeats one start time, stop time and label (OL_L_1.dat). The sample series below shows that these are real trials with their own times.

The 611 repeated rows of 489 are 305 two-second turns alternating with 306 straight runs that end at 100 cm, over 3683 to 6218 s, while the table labels all of them OL_L at one time. Of the 305 turns, 256 go to the right and 49 to the left at 1 s, so the label is wrong for most of them and the turn type of each cannot be read from the file. These rows are left out of every analysis; the session's labelled trials are its first 1000 rows (500 straight, 249 OL_L, 251 OL_R). That these are the 1000 trials of Table S1 is an assumption; the table-s1 section also counts all 1611 rows.

for s, d in S.items():
    tr, beh, seg, samp = d["trials"], d["beh"], d["seg"], d["samples"]
    dt = np.diff(beh.ts.values)
    print(f"session {s}: {len(beh)} samples; timestamp step {np.median(dt):.4f} s ({1 / np.median(dt):.0f} Hz, SI: 500 Hz);"
          f" steps that go back in time: {(dt < 0).sum()}")
    for c in ["d_for", "d_lat", "v_for", "v_lat"]:
        v = beh[c].values
        print(f"  {c}: {np.nanmin(v):.2f} to {np.nanmax(v):.2f}, median {np.nanmedian(v):.2f}, NaN {np.isnan(v).mean():.4f}")
    it = tr[tr.intact]
    cl = it.index[it.label == "CL"]
    print(f"  straight rows: forward distance at the end median {samp.d_for_end[cl].median():.1f} cm "
          f"(5th to 95th percentile {samp.d_for_end[cl].quantile(.05):.1f} to {samp.d_for_end[cl].quantile(.95):.1f});"
          f" duration median {samp.t_local_end[cl].median():.2f} s")
    # forward distance against the integral of forward speed, per straight row
    ratio = []
    for r in cl[samp.d_for_end[cl].values > 50]:
        idx = seg[r]
        t = beh.t_local.values[idx]
        v = np.nan_to_num(beh.v_for.values[idx])
        ratio.append(np.trapezoid(v, t) / max(beh.d_for.values[idx][-1], 1e-9))
    print(f"  {np.sum(samp.d_for_end[cl] <= 50)} straight rows end before 50 cm. Over the others, integral of v_for / forward distance: median {np.median(ratio):.3f}"
          f" (5th to 95th percentile {np.percentile(ratio, 5):.3f} to {np.percentile(ratio, 95):.3f})")

The ball tracking is sampled at 500 Hz, as the SI states. Forward distance restarts at each trial and the straight rows end at 100 cm (the "100cm" of their labels), so distances are in cm. Over the straight rows that reach 50 cm, the integral of speed_for_smooth over the row equals its forward distance (median ratio 1.00), so speeds are in cm/s on the same clock. In 503, 169 straight rows end before 50 cm (5 in 489), and its straight rows last a median 10.00 s against 4.82 s in 489. Lateral distance also restarts at 0 at each trial.

Do the behavioural samples share the clock of the trials table? Below, the trial type (OL_L against OL_R) is decoded from lateral position at single times around the stored turn starts, and from all samples after the start with the true labels and with labels shifted by one OL trial.

In [6]:
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
for s, d in S.items():
    tr, beh, seg = d["trials"], d["beh"], d["seg"]
    ol = tr[tr.intact & tr.label.str.startswith("OL")]
    y = (ol.label == "OL_L").values.astype(int)
    rows = list(ol.index)
    grid = np.arange(-0.5, 1.0001, 0.1)
    X = np.array([[bv._on_grid(beh, seg[r], "d_lat", np.array([t]))[0] if t >= 0 else
                   bv._on_grid(beh, seg[r - 1], "d_lat", np.array([t + beh.t_local.values[seg[r - 1]][-1]]))[0]
                   for t in grid] for r in rows])
    X = np.nan_to_num(X)
    acc = {f"{t:+.1f}": bv.decode_accuracy(X[:, [k]], y, rng) for k, t in enumerate(grid)}
    shifted = bv.decode_accuracy(X[:, grid > 0], np.roll(y, 1), rng)
    true = bv.decode_accuracy(X[:, grid > 0], y, rng)
    print(f"session {s}: OL_L against OL_R from lateral position (cm) in single 0.1 s samples, accuracy by time from the turn start:")
    print("  ", {k: round(v, 2) for k, v in acc.items()})
    print(f"   from all samples after the start: true labels {true:.3f}; labels shifted by one OL trial {shifted:.3f};"
          f" chance {max(y.mean(), 1 - y.mean()):.3f}")

The trial type cannot be decoded before or at the stored start (accuracy 0.42 to 0.56 from -0.5 to 0.2 s) and becomes decodable from 0.3 to 0.4 s on (0.93 and 0.98 at 1 s); with the labels shifted by one trial accuracy falls to chance. Lateral position therefore shares the clock of the trials table, and OL_L trials turn to the positive (left) side, as the labels say.

All units pass the SI's quality thresholds. unit_type (Excitatory, Inhibitory) is the 0.4 ms waveform duration rule of the SI: Inhibitory equals duration below 0.4 ms for 61 of 61 units of 489 and 42 of 43 of 503. 489 has 61 units (Table S1: 65), with 7 in L2/3 and 12 in L6 where Fig. 5B gives 10 and 13, and 30 FS and 31 RS where Fig. 5B gives 43 and 22. 503 has 43 units (Table S1: 48), three of them labelled WM, a layer the paper does not use. Unit 101 of 489, the paper's 489101, is labelled Inhibitory, L5A, waveform duration 0.2 ms (FS by the SI's rule), while the paper calls it RS; it is the session's highest-rate unit (37.6 Hz), as the paper says of 489101. The spikes of 489 run to 6255 s, past the end of its trials table (3683 s) and its behaviour (6218 s); those of 503 run to 7326 s, past the end of its behaviour (7297 s).

The spikes have to share the trial clock for any neural claim. The paper describes, for 489, a sharp peak at 0.026 s, a suppression to about a third of the baseline rate and a ramp in OL_L trials only, in all units. Below, the population rate around the stored onsets, and the decoding of trial type from per-unit spike counts.

for s, d in S.items():

    st = f["units/spike_times"][:]
    per_unit = np.split(st, idx[:-1])
    ol = tr[tr.intact & tr.label.str.startswith("OL")]
    y = (ol.label == "OL_L").values.astype(int)
    res = {}
    for name, (a, b) in {"-0.5 to 0 s": (-0.5, 0), "0 to 0.5 s": (0, 0.5), "0.5 to 1.8 s": (0.5, 1.8)}.items():
        X = np.array([[np.searchsorted(x, t0 + b) - np.searchsorted(x, t0 + a) for x in per_unit] for t0 in ol.start_time.values], float)
        acc = bv.decode_accuracy(X, y, rng)
        null = [bv.decode_accuracy(X, rng.permutation(y), rng) for _ in range(20)]
        res[name] = f"{acc:.3f} (shuffled labels {np.mean(null):.3f}, 95th percentile {np.percentile(null, 95):.3f})"
    print(f"session {s}: OL_L against OL_R from per-unit spike counts at the stored onsets: {res}")

At the stored onsets there is no trial-locked response. The population rate stays within 5.8 to 10.8 Hz over -1 to 2 s, with a baseline SD of 0.41 to 0.50 Hz over 5 ms bins. The lowest bin of the suppression window (0.065 to 0.14 s) is 6.43 to 8.49 Hz, at least 86% of the baseline (489 OL_L: 6.43 against 7.48 Hz), where the paper has the rate of 489 fall from 2 to 0.7 Hz. In 489 the largest bin of the ramp window is below the largest bin elsewhere in -1 to 2 s (OL_L 8.01 against 8.69 Hz, OL_R 7.46 against 8.32 Hz). In 503 OL_R the ramp-window maximum (10.78 Hz) is the maximum of the whole range, 1.83 Hz above the baseline. Trial type cannot be decoded from the units' spike counts in any window (0.460 to 0.522, against shuffled-label 95th percentiles of 0.521 to 0.542), although the animal's lateral position decodes it at 0.920 to 0.954.

The spikes may be offset from the trial clock. The tables below search for the offset two ways: the lag of the largest onset-triggered deviation of the population rate, per window of about 40 onsets, with a null from onsets drawn at random, and the lag of the largest correlation between the population rate and running speed, per 400 s window. Neither uses the shape of the paper's response. In 503, a straight-line clock fitted to the speed lags is then used as a coarse check.

print(f"503 speed clock from the {np.sum(sp_tab.r >= 0.25)} of {len(sp_tab)} windows with r >= 0.25 (trial clock {span[0]:.0f} to"
      f" {span[1]:.0f} s): lag = {icpt:.2f} s + {slope * 1000:.2f} ms per s; residual SD {resid_sd:.2f} s")
ol = tr[tr.intact & tr.label.str.startswith("OL")]
ol = ol[(ol.start_time >= span[0]) & (ol.start_time <= span[1])]
y = (ol.label == "OL_L").values.astype(int)
on = ol.start_time.values + icpt + slope * ol.start_time.values

per_unit = np.split(d["file"]["units/spike_times"][:], idx[:-1])
for name, (a, b) in {"-0.5 to 0 s": (-0.5, 0), "0 to 0.5 s": (0, 0.5), "0.5 to 1.8 s": (0.5, 1.8)}.items():
    X = np.array([[np.searchsorted(x, t0 + b) - np.searchsorted(x, t0 + a) for x in per_unit] for t0 in on], float)
    acc = bv.decode_accuracy(X, y, rng)
    nl = [bv.decode_accuracy(X, rng.permutation(y), rng) for _ in range(20)]
    print(f"decoding OL_L against OL_R from per-unit counts, {name} on the speed clock: {acc:.3f} (shuffled labels mean"
          f" {np.mean(nl):.3f}, 95th percentile {np.percentile(nl, 95):.3f})")

The spikes cannot be placed on the trial clock at the precision the claims need. In 489 only 2 of the 12 windows of the onset-triggered search exceed the 95th percentile of the null (4.78). Their best lags are not random, though: in windows 0 to 6 they rise almost steadily (4.36, 6.81, 7.50, 7.37, 9.57, 10.93, 12.23 s), and the first two speed windows agree (5.50 and 5.85 s), which suggests a drifting offset like that of 503. Windows 7 to 11 depart from that trend (17.04, 15.04, 10.56, 43.31, 26.02 s). The speed correlations of 489 are weak (|r| at most 0.17) and change sign after 1200 s, so they do not give a clock, and no window's z separates its lag from chance; any clock drawn from these lags would be no finer than that of 503. In 503 the lag is found. The onset-triggered search exceeds the null's 95th percentile (5.04) in 10 of 12 windows, and the speed correlation gives a lag that grows smoothly from 12.9 to 19.75 s over 0 to 5200 s (r 0.29 to 0.62). A straight line through those 13 windows (11.86 s plus 1.37 ms per s) leaves a residual SD of 0.56 s. The onset-triggered lags of the seven windows in its span agree with it only loosely: windows 1 and 2 (11.78 and 14.15 s) lie within 1.5 s of it (13.24 and 14.19 s), window 3 (12.07 against 15.23 s) is 3.2 s off, about 6 residual SDs, and windows 0 and 4 to 6 (5.58, 52.54, 19.92, 21.91 s against 12.33, 16.26, 17.22, 18.13 s) are 2.7 to 36.3 s off. On this speed clock the 319 OL trials of 503 in its span show direction-specific responses beyond the null of random onsets (-0.22 to +0.25 Hz in 0 to 0.3 s, -0.25 to +0.26 Hz in 0.3 to 1.8 s): OL_L rises by 1.38 Hz in 0 to 0.3 s, and OL_R falls by 0.82 and 1.89 Hz. Trial type decodes from per-unit counts at 0.865 (0 to 0.5 s) and 0.912 (0.5 to 1.8 s) against shuffled 95th percentiles of 0.552 and 0.535, but also at 0.655 before the onset, which may come from the clock error mixing post-onset spikes into the baseline. The clock was fitted to running speed, and running differs by trial type in 503 (1.7% of OL_L rows against 31.8% of OL_R rows run, in the figs1-running-speed section), so these responses and the decoding, before and after the onset, may in part reflect running and not a neural response to the turn. So the spike times of 503 are about 12 s later than the trial times of the same events, and the gap grows by about 1.4 ms per s, but it is known only to about half a second. The speed lag also contains the unknown delay between spiking and running. The claims test windows and tolerances of 5 to 180 ms (the 0.026 s peak, the 0.065 to 0.14 s suppression, the 0.12 s ramp onset), so none can be tested on it, and 489, the animal of most claims, has no clock at all. The files hold no synchronisation signal and do not say how spike times relate to the trial times. An alignment fitted to the neural response would set the very timings the claims test, so none is adopted, and every claim that needs spikes at these timings is blocked as metadata_insufficient. The epoch 1 rate of fig1n-epoch-rates is an average over a long window and is tested at every lag below. The behaviour is on the trial clock and its claims are tested.

The behaviour claims use the intact rows: 489 rows 0 to 999 (249 OL_L, 251 OL_R) and all 1027 rows of 503 (230 OL_L, 283 OL_R).

table-s1-recordings¶

The recordings comprise 13 ephys sessions and 6 behaviour-only sessions, one per animal, with the numbers of accepted single units and of trials per animal listed in Table S1, and with the units and OL turn trials of the example sessions given in Fig. 1J-K and Fig. S4.

Criterion: unit counts and the OL_L plus OL_R counts must match exactly, and at least 17 of 19 total trial counts within 10%; partially reproduced when unit counts match for at least 10 of 13 ephys animals. The paper's numbers below are the claims file's.

The trial counts match: 503 has 1027 rows (1027) and 489 has 1000 intact rows (1000). That the intact rows of 489 are the trials of Table S1 is an assumption: counted with its 611 repeated rows, 489 has 1611 trials, outside 10% of 1000, and with the 305 repeated turns given the direction of their displacement, 298 OL_L and 507 OL_R. The 489 layer counts differ from Fig. 5B in L2/3 (7 against 10) and L6 (12 against 13), and its FS and RS counts (30 and 31) differ from Fig. 5B (43 and 22).

fig1n-epoch-rates¶

For animal 489, the population rate is about 2 Hz during straight running before the turn, peaks sharply at t = 0.026 s (epoch 2), drops to about 0.7 Hz (epoch 3) for both turn directions, and, for contralateral turns only, ramps to a maximum at about t = 0.25 s (epoch 4); for ipsilateral turns the suppression lasts to the end of the turn.

Criterion: animal 489, population-averaged rate in Hz (spikes in 5 ms bins, averaged over trials of one type and over units), OL_L and OL_R separately; epoch 1 rate 2.0 ± 0.1 Hz over (a) -0.5 to 0 s or (b) -1 to 0 s; epoch 2 peak time, epoch 3 minimum and epoch 4 maximum time as listed in the claims file. The spikes are not on the trial clock (data check), so the three timed values cannot be tested. The epoch 1 rate is an average over a whole window of straight running, and it can be computed at every alignment the data check found possible: the onsets are shifted by every lag searched in the data check, -20 to 60 s in 0.1 s steps. The mean rate over all CL rows is given as a check that does not depend on where the turn starts.

Result: not reproduced. The epoch 1 rate of 489 is far above 2.0 ± 0.1 Hz at every alignment: over the 801 lags from -20 to 60 s it is 6.65 to 7.80 Hz under reading (a) and 6.74 to 7.75 Hz under reading (b), for both turn types, and none of the 1602 (lag, turn) pairs is within tolerance. At the stored onsets it is 7.15 to 7.48 Hz. Over all CL rows the rate per unit is 7.18 to 7.26 Hz at lags of 0 to 25 s, and 7.09 Hz over the whole recording. The units table gives a mean firing rate of 5.91 Hz (median 2.95 Hz; 19 of 61 units below 2 Hz). The dataset has 61 of the paper's 65 units. The epoch 2 peak time, the epoch 3 minimum and the epoch 4 maximum time need the spikes on the trial clock and are not tested.

Reproduced when the mean is within 4 cm/s of 21 under a reading.

Running trials (mean speed above 10 cm/s) by row type, all rows:

  489: {'CL': '95.6% of 500', 'OL_L': '96.8% of 249', 'OL_R': '92.8% of 251', 'repeated rows': '85.9% of 611'}; Table S1 92.6%

Result: not reproduced. Animal 503 runs at a mean of 5.93 cm/s over all samples (reading a) and 12.95 cm/s over the samples of its running trials (reading b), both outside 17 to 25 cm/s. Reading (c) can use only 2 of the 19 animals; their mean running speed is 16.56 cm/s, also outside. 489 alone (19.98 cm/s) would be inside. The dataset holds no habituation sessions (reading d). Against Table S1, 489 matches (19.98 against 22.2 cm/s; 91.7% running trials against 92.6%), but 503 does not (13.14 against 16.1 cm/s; 27.7% against 52.8%). By row type, 503 runs in 37.0% of its CL rows, 1.7% of its OL_L rows and 31.8% of its OL_R rows, so no choice of rows gives Table S1's 52.8%. With its lower unit count (43 against 48) and OL counts (513 against 609), this suggests that the deposited session or curation of 503 differs from the one the paper analysed.

fig2a-success-rate¶

In the unrewarded task, with a correct trial defined as ±1 cm lateral clearance at t = 1 s, animal 503 succeeds in 95% of 414 randomized turn trials (14 failed trajectories).

Criterion: animal 503, OL trials, lateral position at t = 1 s; zero (e) at t = 0 or (f) at the start of the straight section; trials (a) all OL or (b) the first 414; clearance (c) at least 1 cm in the turn direction or (d) at least 1 cm either way. Reproduced when the success rate is within 10% of 0.95 under a reading. A variant, not in the criterion, uses only OL trials run above 10 cm/s (Table S1's running criterion), since the paper does not say which 414 trials it used.

Result: not reproduced. Under the eight readings of the criterion the success rate is 0.609 to 0.694 (154 to 165 failed trials), against 0.95 (0.855 to 1.045). The failures are trials with almost no lateral movement: the 5th percentile of displacement in the turn direction at 1 s is 0.00 cm for both turn types. Restricted to the 94 OL trials run above 10 cm/s, a variant outside the criterion, the success rate is 0.979 to 1.000 (0 to 2 failures), so the paper's 95% may come from a selection of running trials that the paper does not describe. These 94 trials are almost all OL_R: 503 runs in 1.7% of its 230 OL_L rows and 31.8% of its 283 OL_R rows (figs1-running-speed).

fig2b-lateral-spread¶

Lateral positions are tightly confined during the straight CL section (0.14 ± 0.55 cm, mean ± SD, at t = 0) and their distribution widens over time after the turn (t = 1 s and 3 s), about twice as wide at 3 s as at 2 s (SD 2.30 against 1.49).

Criterion: 503 (Fig. 2B) and 489 (Fig. S6B); lateral distance (a) as stored or (b) integrated from the start of the straight section; the 2 s and 3 s SDs read as (c) 503 at 3 s and 489 at 2 s, (d) both 503, (e) both 489. Reproduced when the t = 0 values and the widening hold and the 2 s and 3 s SDs match under one reading; partially when only the t = 0 values and the widening hold. Following the legends, 503 pools OL_L and OL_R (Fig. 2B, "414 trials randomized between OL_L and OL_R") and 489 uses OL_L (Fig. S6A-B); per-direction values for 503 are shown as well.

Result: not reproduced. The stored lateral distance restarts at 0 at every trial, so at t = 0 it is 0.00 ± 0.00 cm by construction (reading a). Integrated from the start of the straight section (reading b), 503 is at 0.20 ± 0.84 cm at t = 0: the mean is within 0.55 cm of 0.14, but the SD is outside 0.55 ± 0.055. Under (b) the distribution widens (SD 0.84, 2.90 and 7.20 cm at 0, 1 and 3 s for 503), but none of the 2 s and 3 s SDs matches 2.30 and 1.49 under (c), (d) or (e) (503: 7.02 and 7.20 cm; 489: 4.06 and 5.40 cm; under (a), 503 0.76 at 3 s and 489 3.50 at 2 s). Every trial has a value at 1, 2 and 3 s, and all but one of 489 at 0 s. Pooling both turn directions widens the 503 distributions; per direction its 3 s SDs are 4.58 (OL_L) and 3.10 (OL_R) cm under (b).

fig4-ddm-fit¶

A classical drift-diffusion model fitted to the reaction-time distribution of animal 489 gives a nondecision time of 0.12 s, drift 2.91, bound 0.59 and noise 0.25 (BIC -664); a generalized DDM with collapsing bounds and leak fits better (BIC -705), with normalized drift K/B of 11.12.

Criterion: animal 489, OL_L trials ((e) the 266 of Fig. 4B or (f) the 520 of Fig. S7C-D; the dataset's labelled OL_L trials are 249, and all are used); RT as in fig2i-ft-rt: the largest peak after t = 0 of (c) the run angle derivative or (d) the lateral acceleration, in the turn direction, searched over (e) 0 to 1 s or (f) 0 to 1.8 s; correct as in fig2a-success-rate; PyDDM; (a) sigma free or (b) sigma fixed at 0.25; GDDM with exponentially collapsing bounds and a leaky integrator. Reproduced when NDT is within 10% of 0.12 s and the GDDM BIC is below the DDM BIC under a reading; partially when only one holds. A maximum at the edge of the search window is not a peak, and those trials are dropped (a standard choice, counted below). The first table also gives RT for both ephys animals and both turn types, which fig2i-ft-rt asks for.

Some RTs fall in the first tens of milliseconds, before the leg push the SI says the peak marks ("Such peaks are associated with characteristic push outwards with RH or LH legs", SI, Fitting of drift diffusion models). The paper's histogram of the RTs of 489 (Fig. S7D) has no RT below about 0.2 s. A DDM gives no likelihood to an RT below its NDT, so such RTs can hold the NDT down. The paper does not say how it handled them, so each fit is run three ways (an assumption): (i) all RTs kept, (ii) with a uniform mixture of weight up to 0.1, PyDDM's means "to confer robustness when fitting using likelihood" (OverlayUniformMixture), and (iii) with RTs below 0.1 s dropped. A further cell shows how the NDT moves with a cutoff and with the mixture's limit, and the likelihood profile of NDT.

rt_rows = []
RT = {}
for s, d in S.items():
    tr, beh, seg = d["trials"], d["beh"], d["seg"]
    for lab, sg in [("OL_L", 1), ("OL_R", -1)]:
        rws = list(tr.index[tr.intact & (tr.label == lab)])
        x1 = bv.lateral_at(beh, seg, rws, 1.0)
        for sig in ["angle", "acc"]:
            for w in [(0.0, 1.0), (0.0, 1.8)]:
                rt = np.array([bv.reaction_time(beh, seg[r], sg, sig, w) for r in rws])
                edge = (rt <= w[0] + bv.RT_DT) | (rt >= w[1] - bv.RT_DT) | np.isnan(rt)
                RT[(s, lab, sig, w)] = (rt, edge, x1, sg)

handlings = {"none": None, "uniform mixture": "mixture", "RT < 0.1 s dropped": 0.1}
jobs = []
for sig in ["angle", "acc"]:
    for w in [(0.0, 1.0), (0.0, 1.8)]:
        rt, edge, x1, sg = RT[("489", "OL_L", sig, w)]
        for clear, correct in [("c", sg * x1 >= 1), ("d", np.abs(x1) >= 1)]:
            for hname, h in handlings.items():
                keep = ~edge & ~np.isnan(x1)
                if isinstance(h, float):
                    keep &= rt >= h
                for sigma_free in [True, False]:
                    for model in ["DDM", "GDDM"]:
                        if model == "GDDM" and (sigma_free or w[1] > 1.0):
                            continue   # GDDM fitted on the sigma 0.25 readings of the 0 to 1 s window only
                        key = (sig, f"{w[0]:g}-{w[1]:g}", clear, "a: sigma free" if sigma_free else "b: sigma 0.25", hname, model)
                        jobs.append((key, rt[keep], correct[keep], model, sigma_free, w[1], 0.1 if h == "mixture" else 0.0))
t_fit = time.time()

# How the DDM nondecision time depends on the handling of early RTs (sigma 0.25, clearance c)
jobs2 = []
for sig in ["angle", "acc"]:
    for w in [(0.0, 1.0), (0.0, 1.8)]:
        rt, edge, x1, sg = RT[("489", "OL_L", sig, w)]
        keep = ~edge & ~np.isnan(x1)
        correct = sg * x1 >= 1
        for cut in [0.05, 0.1, 0.15, 0.2]:
            m = keep & (rt >= cut)
            jobs2.append((("cutoff", sig, f"{w[0]:g}-{w[1]:g}", cut), rt[m], correct[m], "DDM", False, w[1], 0.0))
        jobs2.append((("mixture up to 0.3", sig, f"{w[0]:g}-{w[1]:g}", None), rt[keep], correct[keep], "DDM", False, w[1], 0.3))
rt, edge, x1, sg = RT[("489", "OL_L", "angle", (0.0, 1.0))]
keep = ~edge & ~np.isnan(x1)
for ndt in [0.0, 0.03, 0.06, 0.09, 0.12, 0.15]:
    jobs2.append((("profile", "angle", "0-1", ndt), rt[keep], (sg * x1 >= 1)[keep], "DDM", False, 1.0, 0.1, ndt))
with Pool(4) as pool:
    fits2 = dict(pool.map(bv.fit_ddm, jobs2))
sens = pd.DataFrame([dict(test=k[0], signal=k[1], window=k[2], value=k[3], n=len(j[1]), min_RT=j[1].min(), **fits2[k])
                     for j in jobs2 for k in [j[0]]])
cutt = sens[sens.test == "cutoff"]
print("DDM fits with RTs below a cutoff dropped:")
print(cutt[["signal", "window", "value", "n", "min_RT", "NDT", "K", "B", "BIC"]].round(3).to_string(index=False))
gap = cutt.min_RT - cutt.NDT
print(f"NDT minus the smallest RT kept: {(-gap).min():.3f} to {(-gap).max():.3f} s; NDT within 0.108 to 0.132 s in "
      f"{np.sum((cutt.NDT - 0.12).abs() <= 0.012)} of {len(cutt)} fits")
print("\nDDM fits with a uniform mixture of weight up to 0.3:")
print(sens[sens.test == "mixture up to 0.3"][["signal", "window", "n", "NDT", "mixture", "K", "B", "BIC"]].round(3).to_string(index=False))
prof = sens[sens.test == "profile"]

Result: partially reproduced. No reading gives a DDM nondecision time within 0.108 to 0.132 s: it is 0.000 to 0.005 s with all RTs kept, 0.000 to 0.039 s with the uniform mixture and 0.080 to 0.094 s with RTs below 0.1 s dropped (16 fits each). The GDDM BIC is below the DDM BIC in all 4 readings fitted with all RTs kept (-201.6 to -76.8 against 42.7 to 82.8) and with RTs below 0.1 s dropped (-441.5 to -343.8 against -298.4 to -266.4), but in none of the 4 with the mixture (-432.9 to -298.5 against -441.8 to -300.0). So only the GDDM condition holds, and only when the early RTs are not absorbed by the mixture.

The NDT is not well determined by these data. With all RTs kept it sits under the smallest RT (0.007 s). When RTs below a cutoff are dropped it follows the cutoff, 0.011 to 0.030 s under the smallest RT kept, so one of 16 cutoff fits (0.129 s, lateral acceleration, 0 to 1.8 s, cutoff 0.15 s) lands within tolerance because of the cutoff chosen, which is why these fits are shown as a check and not as readings. With the mixture, which lets the NDT move free of any cutoff, it stays at 0.000 to 0.039 s (0.003 to 0.028 s with a weight up to 0.3). The fitted mixture weight is at its limit of 0.1 in all 16 DDM fits (one GDDM fit is at 0.099); with a limit of 0.3 it is 0.158 to 0.243, below the limit but far above the 3 to 5% of OL_L RTs below 0.1 s (8 to 13 of 249). So the mixture absorbs more than the early RTs, which suggests the plain DDM misfits the shape of the RT distribution more broadly, and adds to the low confidence in this outcome. In the likelihood profile, NDT fixed at 0.12 s gives a BIC 4.4 above the best, at 0 s. The profile fits have the same number of parameters, so 4.4 is a deviance difference, and 0.12 s lies just outside a 95% profile-likelihood interval (p about 0.04): it is narrowly excluded.

The other values are also far from the paper's. DDM BIC is 42.7 to 205.9 with all RTs, -441.8 to -173.0 with the mixture and -298.4 to -119.4 with the cutoff (paper -664, none within tolerance); GDDM BIC is at best -441.5 (paper -705); bound B is within tolerance of 0.59 in 1 of 48 DDM fits; K/B is 0.30 to 4.06 (11.12). Drift K is within tolerance in 6, 4 and 0 of 16 fits under the three handlings; with sigma free, K, B and sigma trade off (only their ratios are identified). The GDDM leak is at the -10 edge of its range in all four fits with all RTs (-10.00 to -9.93), and at 2.50 to 9.99 under the other two handlings; with the cutoff it is 6.04 to 9.99, two of the four fits near the +10 edge. The GDDM was fitted only under sigma 0.25 and the 0 to 1 s window (4 of 16 readings per handling). Since the NDT condition fails in every reading, GDDM fits in the other readings could not change the outcome.

Blocked claims¶

Spike clock (metadata_insufficient). fig1lm-staged-modulation, fig1jk-all-units, fig1n-ramp-slope, fig1o-trial-end-ramp, fig1-ramp-contralateral-only, fig2m-dimensionality-collapse, fig4b-ddm-matches-ramp, fig5e-slope-across-animals, fig4f-varce-example-unit, fig4g-varce-population, fig4j-corce, fig4k-streak-index, fig5b-epochs-in-subpopulations, fig5cd-other-animals and fig5e-principal-vs-neighbor all analyse spikes aligned to the turn onset at a precision of 5 to 180 ms. The data check shows that the spikes are not on the clock of the trials table, that the onset lags of 489 suggest a drifting offset but give no clock (no window's lag is separated from chance and the speed correlations are weak), and that the alignment found for 503 from running speed is known only to about 0.56 s. The claims that compare animals also lack 5 of their 7 animals (only 489 and 503 are in the dataset). Parts of these claims that need no clock are counts: 489 has 61 units and 500 labelled OL trials, where fig1jk-all-units gives 65 and 531, and its layer and FS/RS counts differ from those of fig5b-epochs-in-subpopulations (table-s1-recordings section). These counts describe the recording, not the claims' findings, which stay untested.

Data not in the dataset (data_missing). fig2c-psychometric and fig2d-turn-angle need the psychometric animals (474, 475, 499, 518) and the OL wall distance; fig2f-whisking-params, fig2i-ft-rt, fig2-epoch2-at-first-touch, fig3-wall-kinematics, fig3c-touch-statistics, fig3ijkl-whisking-across-epochs and fig3-not-sensory-drive need whisker tracking, touch times or wall positions, none of which are in the files, and animals 573 and 589; fig2jk-glm-mixed-tuning and figs12-tuning-lost-during-decision need animal 579 and the whisker and gait regressors; fig2l-running-vs-sitting is judged on animal 480. The paper names no other archive for these data. For fig2i-ft-rt the RTs of 489 and 503 are in the fig4-ddm-fit section, but the claim's animals and first-touch times are not in the dataset.

Summary¶

Claim Outcome
table-s1-recordings not reproduced
fig1n-epoch-rates not reproduced (epoch 1 rate; the timed values not tested)
figs1-running-speed not reproduced
fig2a-success-rate not reproduced
fig2b-lateral-spread not reproduced
fig4-ddm-fit partially reproduced
15 claims on trial-aligned spikes blocked: metadata_insufficient
12 claims on whisker, touch, wall, gait or absent animals blocked: data_missing

A failure to reproduce here may be a failure of this attempt, not of the paper: see the reasoning and the differences from the paper's method.

How the analysis differs from the paper's. Only animals 489 and 503 are available. In 489 only the first 1000 trials carry usable labels and times (249 OL_L and 251 OL_R, where the paper uses 266 and 265, or 520 OL_L). The paper's trial selections (414 trials of 503, the 266 OL_L of 489) cannot be identified. Reaction-time maxima at the edge of the search window are dropped. The paper does not say how early RTs were handled in the DDM fits; three handlings are run (all kept, a uniform mixture, RTs below 0.1 s dropped). The GDDM was fitted only under the sigma 0.25 readings of the 0 to 1 s window. The epoch 1 rate is tested at every lag from -20 to 60 s, since the spike clock is unknown.

What was found about the dataset.

  • The spike times are not on the clock of the trials table and the files hold no synchronisation signal, though the SI says TTL signals were used to synchronise them. In 489 the onset lags rise from 4.4 to 12.2 s over the first seven windows, but no window's lag is separated from chance and no clock can be fitted. In 503 the spike times are about 12 s later than the trial times and the gap grows by about 1.4 ms per s; on a clock fitted from running speed the trial type decodes from spike counts at 0.87 to 0.91, but that clock is known only to about 0.56 s, and since running differs by trial type in 503 the decoding may in part reflect running.
  • The dataset holds 2 of the paper's 19 animals; no wall positions, whisker tracking, touch times or gait.
  • In 489 the trials table rows 1000 to 1610 repeat one row; 256 of their 305 turns go right although all are labelled OL_L. In both sessions some 60 OL rows have stop times before their start times, and their sample timestamps restart at the previous trial's start.
  • Unit counts (61 and 43) are below Table S1 (65 and 48), and 489's FS and RS counts (30 and 31) differ from Fig. 5B (43 and 22). Unit 489101 is FS by its waveform duration (0.2 ms) and labelled Inhibitory, where the paper calls it RS. 503 has three units labelled WM.
  • The population rate of 489 is 6.65 to 7.80 Hz before the turn at any alignment, where the paper gives 2 Hz.
  • The age of 489 is P63D in the file and 68 days from its date of birth; 503 runs at 13.1 cm/s in 27.7% of trials where Table S1 gives 16.1 cm/s and 52.8%, and in 1.7% of its OL_L trials.
